item.title: Living in the Weimar era of Ruby
item.description: Much has been said about the DHH keynote that he gave at RailsWorld. To me, it was the voice of a person in an existential crisis, but also a very jaded one. “Look how I don’t care anymore, and you should not care either” is not a great message when you are the headline speaker at the conference - let’s call it CareConf - that you have, yourself, lobbied for. The message from the supreme leader was clear: we vibe-rewrote HEY in a more performant way, it worked great, we neither need nor care about Rails anymore. I honestly believe that, instead of amassing even more applause via vitriolic truth-bombing, he could have just left the toy he no longer loves - including its community - in peace. But here is the thing: the rich and famous losing interest in the good stuff does not oblige the rest of us to. If anything, it frees up the room.

item.title: I built a HOCON conformance suite. It found bugs in the reference implementation.
item.description: I have used HOCON in production for years. I like the format because it is readable and it allows config file composition, so it allows simple multi-environment config shared config files overrides minimizing config differences. As a Python developer, my ultimate combo for config management is Pydantic + pyhocon. I like to try new things, so this June my eyes landed on Zig. I wanted to go back to the roots of programming and see what a modern “C” feels like. After reading the language reference I needed a project, and knowing the Java and Python implementations of HOCON don’t fully agree, it gave me an idea: “Zig has a native C interface, so why not write HOCON in Zig and expose it through C shim? Then every language can share one implementation. Magic!” What a simple project I have picked, right? Writing the tokenizer, the abstract syntax tree, the config and the resolution is the beautiful part. But right after the first implementation works, the question comes: am I really compatible? Luckily there is a written spec and a whole internet of examples. Well, it turned out the spec and the reference implementation do not always agree. Here is a basic config that contains an error: hosts = [db1, db2] db3 The spec says an array next to a string in a concatenation is invalid. lightbend/config 1.4.9, the reference implementation, the one the spec was written for, gives you this: {"hosts":["db1","db2"]} No error, no warning. db3 is gone. Write it the other way round, db3 [db1, db2], and you get the error you were promised. So before going further with the parser, I wrote down what HOCON is supposed to do. That became a conformance suite: 445 cases, each one a sentence of the spec turned into a config file and the value it must produce. lightbend/config 1.4.9 passes 90% of them, pyhocon 70%. My Zig parser, zig-hocon, 69%, and from here on it is built against the suite.

item.description: I have a conjecture which I’m almost certain is true. item.title: GLM-Legal: Advancing Agentic Legal Intelligence
item.description: Large language models are shifting from single-turn code generation toward broader professional collaboration (Professional Cowork). Real-world knowledge work introduces distinct requirements: models must digest fragmented source files under concrete objectives and tight delivery constraints, structure specialized knowledge into cohesive analysis, and maintain domain rigor across the full execution lifecycle. Legal work concentrates on these challenges, providing an ideal stress test for training models to operate in high-stakes professional environments.
